result.summary: Zeus punishes Prometheus for stealing fire by having Hephaestus and Athene fashion the first woman as a beautiful evil for men, and the poet reflects on marriage. The narrative then turns to the Hundred-Handers, whom Zeus freed on Earth's advice to help him against the Titans.

scenes.title: Fire stolen, woman fashioned
scenes.summary: Zeus, angry at Prometheus's theft of fire, has the Limping God mould a maiden of earth. Athene dresses her and the crown is adorned.
scenes.stakes: Mankind faces an evil sent as the price for stolen fire; Prometheus has angered Zeus.

scenes.title: The evil presented to men
scenes.summary: The woman is brought before gods and men, who marvel. The poet explains that women are a trouble to men, whether he marries or not, and that Prometheus could not escape Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Men must suffer evil whether they marry or stay single.

place.name: the place of gods and men

scenes.title: Hundred-Handers freed for war
scenes.summary: Zeus had bound Obriareus, Cottus and Gyes under the earth; Earth advises the gods to free them. They are fed nectar and ambrosia in the ten-year war with the Titans.
scenes.stakes: The gods risk an endless stalemate against the Titans.

place.name: under the wide-pathed earth; Olympus and Othyrs

scenes.title: Zeus rallies Cottus
scenes.summary: Zeus asks the freed brothers to fight the Titans; Cottus pledges their aid.
scenes.stakes: Victory in the war against the Titans depends on the Hundred-Handers.

alias_notes.explanation: An epithet of the lame smith god; the name Hephaestus is not used in this section.
Pallas is a common epithet of Athene.

notable_quotes.reason: Hesiod's famous, misogynistic claim that womankind descends from the first woman, Pandora (unnamed here).
Memorable bee-and-drone simile comparing women to drones.

analysis.text: The passage shows that Zeus's will cannot be evaded: theft of fire is answered with a lasting evil, and rebels are bound while helpers are rewarded.
Its view of women reflects the attitudes of archaic Greek farming society, in which marriage was an economic matter and heirs mattered.

legacy.text: This is the earliest account of the story later known as Pandora, whose name Hesiod gives in Works and Days.

fun_facts.text: Hesiod does not name the first woman here; Pandora appears in his Works and Days.

language_notes.text: "So, sir" is ironic, mocking address; Zeus sarcastically notes that Prometheus still has his tricks, referring to the earlier deception at the sacrifice.
"Melian" refers to the race of men born from ash trees (meliai, ash-tree nymphs); the footnote number is an editorial marker.
Fennel stalk: a hollow giant fennel stem, whose pithy core could carry a smouldering ember.
"Broidered" means embroidered; "girded" means belted or fastened her dress.
"Beautiful evil" is a deliberate paradox: the woman looks lovely but is the price for the blessing of fire.
"No helpmeets in hateful poverty, but only in wealth" means wives share a man's prosperity but give no help in hard times.
"Skeps" are straw beehives; "drones" are male bees that do no work.
"Comeliness" means good looks or handsomeness; "manhood" here means manly vigor or courage.
"Their father" is Heaven (Uranus), who bound his monstrous children; the translation does not name him in this sentence.
"Vaunt" means to boast; the victory would give the gods a glorious reason to boast.
Othyrs is a mountain in Thessaly where the Titans made their stand, set against the gods on Olympus.
"Provided those three with all things fitting" means Zeus gave them proper food and care; nectar and ambrosia are the gods' own food.
"Chill doom" means grim, deadly destruction; Cottus credits Zeus with saving the gods from it.

context_notes.text: The Limping God is Hephaestus, divine smith and craftsman. The woman he moulds is Pandora, though this passage does not name her.
Athene (Pallas Athene) is goddess of wisdom and crafts, especially weaving, so she fittingly clothes the woman.
Prometheus was bound by Zeus in chains as punishment, a story Hesiod tells just before this passage.
The son of Cronos is Zeus. Earth (Gaia) is his grandmother and advises him because she is the mother of the Hundred-Handers.
This ten-year war is the Titanomachy, the gods' struggle against the Titans for rule of the cosmos.
Zeus calls the Hundred-Handers children of Earth and Heaven, which makes them brothers of the Titans they are about to fight.

literary_notes.text: "Limping God" and later "very famous" identify Hephaestus by his defining trait, as Homeric-style epithets do.
Gods and men marvel at something beautiful that is in truth "sheer guile"; admiration hides the harm.
Hesiod compares women to idle drones fed by industrious bees, casting men as the toiling bees; the comparison expresses his misogynistic view.
Marriage brings sorrow, but so does staying single; the balanced dilemma shows no escape from the "second evil."
The war's outcome "hung evenly balanced" like weights on a scale, conveying the stalemate.
Zeus appeals to gratitude, reminding the brothers of their rescue to bind them to his cause.
The closing address "O lord, son of Cronos" gives formal deference, marking Cottus's loyalty to Zeus.
